The frequency knob and field set the frequency of the oscillator (the default is 1 kHz), and you can double-tap this field and enter a value ranging from 1 Hz to 22 kHz.

downgrades.title: Compressor — switch the model, not just the settings
downgrades.reason: The evidence_quote is reconstructed, not quoted. Apple's Compressor main parameters page (lgcead9636ef) describes circuit types generically and never names third-party hardware: its actual Studio FET text is 'Field Effect Transistor compressors are known for their fast transient response. They can deliver a clean or colored tone (particularly in the midrange)... FET compressors are ideal for drums, vocals, guitars, and other signals with a fast attack phase' — not 'Emulates the Universal Audio 1176'. Worse, the auditor's 'Vintage Opto: ...known for their fast transient response... ideal for vocals and guitars' is that same Studio FET description reattributed to a different circuit type (optical compressors are the slow-responding ones), so the quote is internally corrupt. 'Vintage VCA: Based on the SSL buss compressor' likewise appears nowhere in Apple's text. Only the seven circuit-type names survive; every character/brand equivalence the trick actually trades on is unsourced. SALVAGE: keep 'Compressor is seven compressors in one — the Circuit Type menu at the top swaps the whole detection model, so audition Platinum Digital, Studio VCA, Studio FET, Classic VCA, Vintage VCA, Vintage FET and Vintage Opto on the same source before touching ratio or attack. Apple's own descriptions for each type are in the Compressor main parameters page.' Delete the 1176 / SSL / LA-2A equivalences and the per-type adjectives unless each is separately sourced.

downgrades.title: Limiter — set it as a safety, not a loudness tool
downgrades.reason: Two failures. First, the auditor's own reason concedes 'The specific 0.5 dB and 3 dB figures are unsourced editorial rules of thumb, not documented specs' — a trick cannot be VERIFIED while its only numeric, checkable content is admitted to be unsourced; that is the definition of UNVERIFIABLE, and 'taste rather than a refundable factual error' is not one of the available verdicts. Second, the quoted Apple sentence arguably cuts against the headline: Apple says Limiter 'raises the overall volume of the signal so that it reaches, but does not exceed, 0 dB' — i.e. Apple documents it as a loudness tool applied last, which does not support 'set it as a safety, NOT a loudness tool' as written. The evidence supports the placement claim only. SALVAGE: 'Apple documents Limiter as belonging at the very end of the chain: it is "typically applied as the very last process in the mastering signal chain, where it raises the overall volume of the signal so that it reaches, but does not exceed, 0 dB". Put it last, after your EQ and bus compression, and set the Output Level to the ceiling you want the master to respect.' Drop the 0.5 dB and 3 dB figures entirely, or label them explicitly as personal preference rather than spec.

downgrades.title: Channel EQ — drag the band’s vertical line sideways to set Q
downgrades.reason: The evidence_quote splices non-Apple text into a single quote attributed to one Apple URL. Searching the exact sentence 'If you ever need to reset a band entirely, simply Option-click it to restore it to its default settings' surfaces it in third-party Channel EQ blog write-ups (woodyardmusic, logicxx), and its conversational register ('If you ever need to... simply...') is not Apple guide style — Apple's pages use imperative parameter-table prose. So the Option-click-to-reset element rests on a single blog, which the audit rules say is not sufficient alone. On top of that, the auditor cleared 'double-click a gain value to type it exactly' with the reasoning 'standard Logic numeric-field behaviour and carries no risk' — that is precisely the assume-it-because-everyone-knows-it reasoning the brief bans as the bug. Only the Q half is genuinely Apple-sourced (Apple does document dragging the vertical lines that encompass the band to adjust Q only). SALVAGE: 'To change a band's Q without touching its gain or frequency, drag the vertical lines that encompass the selected band in the Channel EQ display — that adjusts the Q (bandwidth) only. Holding Command while dragging a band constrains the movement to one axis, so you can change frequency without nudging gain.' Cut the Option-click reset and the double-click-to-type line unless each can be pinned to an Apple page.

downgrades.title: Linear Phase EQ on the master, Channel EQ everywhere else
downgrades.reason: The auditor concedes in their own reason that 'Apple does not say "more CPU" in those words' and that the comparative sources 'agree it is the heavier plug-in' — but supplies no URL or quote for any of those comparative sources, so under the two-independent-sources rule none of them count. The CPU claim is not incidental: 'Channel EQ everywhere else' is the trick's whole recommendation, and CPU cost is the stated reason for it. Note also that the Apple fact the auditor gestures at — that Linear Phase EQ uses a fixed amount of CPU regardless of how many bands are active — is not the same proposition as 'Linear Phase EQ costs more CPU than Channel EQ', and on a track using few bands it points the other way. SALVAGE: 'Linear Phase EQ and Channel EQ are not the same plug-in with a different skin. Apple: Linear Phase EQ "preserves the phase of the audio signal", whereas Channel EQ "can introduce phase shifts of the signal that can have an audible (and often desirable) effect on the sound" — and Linear Phase EQ "introduces greater amounts of latency". Reach for Linear Phase EQ where phase coherency matters most and latency is tolerable (mastering, parallel/multi-mic material); use Channel EQ where you want the colour and the low latency.' Drop the CPU comparison unless it can be sourced.

downgrades.title: Vintage EQ Collection — three genuinely different colours
downgrades.reason: The quote supports the three plug-in names, the eras, and 'add color to your productions' — but not the trick's operative claim. The auditor's reason states the evidence 'supports the "character even with the controls flat" claim' via 'its own named output stage (Smooth / Punchy / Silky)' — those three words appear nowhere in the quoted text and no source is given for them; they were supplied from the auditor's memory and then used as the bridge to the conclusion. That is exactly the reconstruct-then-cite failure mode. 'Distinct tonal characteristics of the original units' is a general marketing sentence and does not establish that the plug-ins colour a signal at neutral settings, which is the falsifiable mechanism a buyer would test. SALVAGE: 'Logic ships three modelled vintage EQs — Vintage Tube EQ, Vintage Graphic EQ and Vintage Console EQ — recreating classic units from the 50s, 60s and 70s that, in Apple's words, "feature the distinct tonal characteristics of the original units". They are not interchangeable with Channel EQ: try the same boost on all three and pick by ear.' Remove the claim that they colour with the controls flat, and remove the Smooth/Punchy/Silky output-stage names unless each can be pinned to Apple's parameter pages.

downgrades.title: Space Designer — load your own impulse responses
downgrades.reason: Version mismatch — the exact failure mode the brief warns about. The quoted sentence 'Any mono, stereo, AIFF, SDII, or WAV file can be used as an IR' is Logic 9-era manual text (it survives at help.apple.com/logicpro/mac/9.1.6/.../chapter_12_section_2.html), not the current page the auditor cited. The live Apple 'Use impulse responses in Logic Pro for Mac' page reads instead: 'Any mono or stereo AIFF or WAVE file can be used as an impulse response. In addition, surround formats up to 7.1, discrete audio files, and B-format audio files that consist of a single surround impulse response can be used.' SDII (Sound Designer II) is gone and the surround/B-format capability is new — so the auditor's proposed 'tightening' would print a fifteen-year-old format list into a book covering 10.7 / 11 / 12. The Sampled IR > Load IR route itself is plausible but was cleared on the same stale page, so it needs re-sourcing against the current guide. SALVAGE: 'Space Designer is a convolution reverb, so it will play back any impulse response you give it, not just Apple's. Apple: "Any mono or stereo AIFF or WAVE file can be used as an impulse response", plus surround formats up to 7.1 and B-format files. Click the Sampled IR button above the main display, then use the IR pop-up menu to load your own file.' Do not tell readers SDII works, and do not say "any audio file" — MP3 and M4A are not on Apple's list.

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked throughout; 17 searches spent, aimed at the falsifiable items (key commands, menu paths, option names, bounce/export mechanics). Snippets quoting the Apple Logic Pro User Guide settled most of them. Three items rest partly on non-Apple sources and are flagged in their reasons: the Control-B assignment for Bounce Regions in Place (agreement across three third-party shortcut references, not found on an Apple page), the "no key command inserts a specific plug-in" finding (Apple documents only the manual slot workflow; the explicit "it does not exist" statements come from Gearspace/LogicProHelp/VI-Control), and "exported tracks start at bar 1" (Apple documents the export length options; the start-position statement comes from Peak-Studios and LogicProHelp). Pure-advice tricks were not searched. Nothing was left unchecked for budget reasons.

tricks.title: Open Key Commands with ⌥K and use the search box
tricks.reason: Apple confirms both halves: Option-K opens the Key Commands window, and that window has a search field for finding commands by name.
tricks.evidence_quote: To open the Key Commands window in Logic Pro, you can choose Logic Pro > Key Commands > Edit (or press Option-K), and the Key Commands window opens. … click All at the top of the window, then enter a search term in the search field.

tricks.title: Export your key commands and back them up
tricks.reason: Version trap. 'Options menu with Export' is the Logic 9-era wording. In the 10.7/11/12 guide the saving and importing of key command sets lives in the Actions pop-up menu at the top left of the Key Commands window, and the export command is 'Save As', not 'Export'. A reader hunting an Options > Export item in a current version will not find it.
tricks.evidence_quote: Click the Actions pop-up menu in the top left of the Key Commands window, then choose Save As. You can save the current key command assignments to any location using the dialog that appears. The default location is ~/Music/Audio Music Apps/Key Commands. … click the Actions pop-up menu in the top left of the Key Commands window, then choose Import Key Commands.
tricks.correction: In the Key Commands window, click the Actions pop-up menu at the top left and choose Save As to write your whole key command set to a file (the default location is ~/Music/Audio Music Apps/Key Commands). Choose Import Key Commands from the same menu to load it back after a reinstall, or on someone else's machine. Losing a year of custom shortcuts to a reinstall is entirely avoidable.

tricks.title: Assign key commands to your most used plugins
tricks.reason: Logic has no key command that inserts a named plug-in on the selected channel. Apple documents only the manual route (click an Audio Effect slot, choose from the pop-up menu); the explicit 'no such key command exists' statements come from three independent Logic forums (Gearspace, LogicProHelp, VI-Control), which also list the real workarounds. A buyer who opens Key Commands and searches for their favourite EQ will find nothing to assign.
tricks.evidence_quote: There are no available key commands for this function, as Logic would need to know which plugin you want to insert and would require multiple key commands—one for each potential plugin slot. … The standard method remains manual: click an Audio Effect slot, then choose a plug-in from the pop-up menu.
tricks.correction: Logic has no key command that inserts a specific plug-in, so get the speed a different way: save the plug-in (or a whole chain) as a channel strip setting and recall it from the channel strip's Settings menu, which inserts every associated plug-in in one click. If you want it on a physical button, assign a controller button to the relevant key command in the Controller Assignments window.

tricks.title: Use Touch Bar or a stream deck for tool switching
tricks.reason: The Touch Bar half is not how Logic works. Apple documents Logic's Touch Bar as a fixed set of Logic-specific screens (Smart Controls, keyboard, drum pads, Configuration/Overview navigation) — there is no facility to put arbitrary assigned key commands on it, so 'any command with a key assignment can be triggered' is false for the Touch Bar. The external-hardware idea is sound for a Stream Deck or a MIDI controller, and Apple does document assigning controller buttons to key commands.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you tap the Smart Controls button in Logic Pro, the following controls appear in the Touch Bar. … When you tap the Keyboard button, you can use the Touch Bar to play the current patch on the selected software instrument track. … When you tap the Drum Pads button, you can use the Touch Bar to play the drums on a Drummer or software instrument track
tricks.correction: Logic's Touch Bar screens are fixed (Smart Controls, keyboard, drum pads, project overview), so you cannot put your own key commands there. For hardware triggering, use a Stream Deck sending the keystroke, or assign a controller button directly to a key command in the Controller Assignments window — search the command by name in the Search field, then press the button. Tools, zoom levels and transport are the highest-value candidates.

tricks.title: Build separate templates for writing, mixing and mastering
tricks.reason: Pure workflow advice about how to organise your own starting points. No menu path, key command, version claim or mechanism assertion to check.

tricks.title: Use Project Alternatives instead of Save As
tricks.reason: The behaviour described is right but the menu path is not what Apple prints. Apple's guide gives the path as File > Project Alternatives, not File > Alternatives. Everything else in the trick (one project, shared assets) is confirmed by the same page.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, choose File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative. … You can create alternative versions of a project, each with a unique name and different settings. … They're saved as part of the project and share the same assets.
tricks.correction: File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative keeps every version inside one project, and Apple's guide is explicit that alternatives "are saved as part of the project and share the same assets" — so you are not duplicating 4 GB of recordings to try a different arrangement.

tricks.title: Turn on “Copy external audio files to project folder”
tricks.reason: The option name and the Assets settings location are both confirmed by Apple, as is the reason given for using it.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose File > Project Settings > Assets (or use the Open Assets Project Settings key command), then select any of the copy checkboxes to copy the respective file types to the project. Files are copied into the project when the project is saved. Saving assets in the project ensures that they are still available when you move or copy the project to another location.

tricks.title: Consolidate before archiving
tricks.reason: Menu path, effect and the archiving use case all match Apple. One small imprecision worth knowing but not worth a refund: Consolidate lets you select which asset types to copy rather than automatically taking every one, and the files land in the project's Media folder.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, choose File > Project Management > Consolidate (or use the Consolidate Project key command). … they are copied to the Media folder inside the project. … This ensures that if you move or copy the project to another computer, or archive the project for later use, the assets remain with the project

tricks.title: Keep a reference track in every project, muted at the top
tricks.reason: Studio-habit advice. Nothing asserted about how Logic behaves that a buyer could test and dispute.

tricks.title: Name your bounce files with the date
tricks.reason: File-naming advice with no claim about Logic's behaviour.

tricks.title: ⌘B bounces the project or the current section
tricks.reason: Command-B and the multi-format claim are both confirmed, but 'Set the locators first and Logic bounces exactly that range' is stated unconditionally and is not. Apple says a bounce covers the whole project by default and that the locators define the bounce range only when Cycle mode is on; otherwise you set the range with the Start and End sliders in the Bounce dialog. A reader who drags the locators with Cycle off gets a full-length bounce.
tricks.evidence_quote: By default, when you bounce a project, the entire project from start to end is bounced, but you can bounce only part of a project by setting the bounce range before performing a bounce. When Cycle mode is on, the bounce range matches the locator positions. … select one or more destination formats in the Destination area.
tricks.correction: File > Bounce > Project or Section, or Command-B. By default Logic bounces the whole project; to bounce a section, turn Cycle mode on and the bounce range matches the locator positions, or set the range directly with the Start and End sliders in the Bounce dialog. Bounce multiple formats in one pass by selecting more than one destination in the Destination area.

tricks.title: Use “Bounce in Place” to commit a track to audio
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the File > Bounce > Track in Place route and the dialog options for effects and for volume/pan. The Control-B assignment for Regions in Place is not printed on the Apple page I could reach (it only says 'or use the corresponding key command'), but three independent third-party shortcut references agree on Control-B, with Control-Command-B for Track in Place — so the trick's ⌃B stands, though it is the weakest-sourced element here.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can choose File > Bounce > Regions in Place (or use the corresponding key command) … File > Bounce, which shows options including Regions in Place, Track in Place, Replace All Tracks, and Project or Section. … Bypass Effect Plug-ins: Select to bypass all plug-ins on the source track during the bounce process. … Include Volume/Pan Automation: Select to have volume and pan automation performed during the bounce process

tricks.title: Export all tracks as audio files for stems
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the exact menu path and one-file-per-track behaviour. The 'all starting at bar 1' part is supported by two independent third-party sources rather than by Apple, and it is the default rather than the only behaviour — the export dialog also offers trimming silence at the end, exporting only the cycle range, and extending file length to the project end, and the cycle-range option would not start at bar 1.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose File > Export > All Tracks as Audio Files. … export all tracks (all audio, software instrument, and Drummer tracks) in a project as audio files—one file per track. … All exported tracks will start at 1 1 1 1 (the project start) when using Export All Tracks as Audio Files.

tricks.title: Turn off “Normalize” when bouncing stems
tricks.reason: The Normalize control and its Off setting exist exactly where the trick says, in the export/bounce dialog, and Off is documented as 'the exported file is not normalized'. The rest is judgement, but the actionable instruction is correct.
tricks.evidence_quote: Off: The exported file is not normalized. Overload Protection Only: Allows downward normalization in case of overloads—levels above 0 dB, which would lead to clipping—but no normalization in case of lower levels. On: The exported file is normalized both for overloads and for lower levels.

tricks.title: Bounce offline unless you have external hardware
tricks.reason: The advice points the right way but two specifics are unsupported. Apple says offline 'can be faster than real time for more complex projects' — not that it always is — and says nothing anywhere I found about offline and realtime bounces being bit-identical, which is the claim a buyer is most likely to challenge. Apple's own limitation is broader than 'outboard gear': only internal sources can be bounced offline, so MIDI tracks and audio channel inputs also force a realtime bounce.
tricks.evidence_quote: Offline bouncing can be faster than real time for more complex projects, and can perform bounces not possible in real time (because they might exceed the processing power of your computer). … Only internal sources (audio or software instrument tracks) can be bounced offline; not MIDI tracks or audio channel inputs.
tricks.salvage: Bounce offline unless something outside the computer is involved. Apple's own wording is that offline bouncing "can be faster than real time for more complex projects, and can perform bounces not possible in real time". Realtime is required when the signal is not purely internal: only audio and software instrument tracks can be bounced offline, not MIDI tracks feeding external instruments or live audio channel inputs.

tricks.title: Add 2 bars of silence at the end of the bounce range
tricks.reason: The tail-clipping advice is sensible but the mechanism as written is conditional and unsourced: the right locator sets the bounce end only when Cycle mode is on, per Apple, and the specific 'two bars' figure has no source. Nobody will refund over the taste part, but they may over dragging the right locator with Cycle off and getting the same clipped tail.
tricks.evidence_quote: By default, when you bounce a project, the entire project from start to end is bounced, but you can bounce only part of a project by setting the bounce range before performing a bounce. When Cycle mode is on, the bounce range matches the locator positions. … adjust the Start and End value sliders.
tricks.salvage: Leave room for the tails. Reverb and delay tails get cut off constantly, so before you bounce, push the End position past the last note — either by adjusting the End value slider in the Bounce dialog, or, with Cycle mode on, by dragging the right locator, since Apple documents that the bounce range matches the locator positions only when Cycle is on. Then listen to the end of the file before you send it.

tricks.title: Colour and name everything before you leave the session
tricks.reason: Session-hygiene advice with no assertion about Logic's behaviour, menus or shortcuts.

tricks.title: Save a version before every major change
tricks.reason: The one checkable element, that New Alternative gives you a safe snapshot to experiment from, is documented by Apple. Note that the menu route is File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative, as flagged on the earlier alternatives trick.
tricks.evidence_quote: Project alternatives let you save snapshots of a project in different states, including different cuts or mixes. … In Logic Pro, choose File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative.

downgrades.title: Turn on “Copy external audio files to project folder”
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own evidence quote never contains the option name — it only says 'select any of the copy checkboxes'. That supports the Assets pane existing, not the named checkbox, which is the whole falsifiable content of the title. I checked Apple's Assets settings page (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/assets-settings-lgcp58b54e81/10.7/mac/11.0, i.e. version-matched to the book's 10.7+ coverage) and the checkboxes are: 'Copy audio files into project' ('If selected, all audio files used in the project are stored as part of your project package or folder'), 'Convert audio file sample rate when importing', 'Copy Sampler audio files into project', 'Copy Alchemy audio files into project', 'Copy Ultrabeat audio files into project', 'Copy Space Designer impulse responses into project'. There is no 'Copy external audio files to project folder' — that is old Logic-era wording, the same failure mode as the non-existent 'As Region Colour' found in sections 1-5. A reader hunting for a checkbox with that name will not find it. SOURCED CORRECTION: retitle to 'Turn on “Copy audio files into project”' and set the body to: 'In File > Project Settings > Assets, select Copy audio files into project — all audio files used in the project are then stored as part of your project package or folder, copied in when the project is saved. Tick the matching boxes for Sampler, Alchemy and Ultrabeat audio and Space Designer impulse responses if you use them. It is the difference between a project that opens on another machine and one that does not.'

downgrades.title: Consolidate before archiving
downgrades.reason: The auditor spotted the defect, wrote it into the reason, and then cleared the trick anyway. The book says Consolidate 'gathers every asset the project depends on into the project package'. Apple's Consolidate page (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/consolidate-assets-in-a-project-lgcpce09b9d8/mac) says you 'select different asset types currently stored outside of your project' and 'In the Consolidate dialog, you select the checkboxes for the asset types you want to copy into the project, then click OK' — it is an opt-in dialog, not an automatic sweep — and the destination is 'the Media folder inside the project', not 'the project package' (a Logic project may be saved as a folder rather than a package). This matters exactly where the trick claims to help: a reader who runs Consolidate expecting everything to come along, and leaves boxes unticked, archives an incomplete project. SOURCED CORRECTION: 'File > Project Management > Consolidate (or the Consolidate Project key command) copies assets stored outside the project into the project''s Media folder. In the Consolidate dialog, tick the checkboxes for every asset type you want brought in — audio files, Sampler/Alchemy/Ultrabeat audio, Space Designer impulse responses, video, and Sound Library content such as Apple Loops — then click OK. Do this before backing up, and check the boxes rather than assuming.'

downgrades.title: Use “Bounce in Place” to commit a track to audio
downgrades.reason: The headline element — the ⌃B in the trick's key field and the first words of the body — has no quoted source. The auditor's evidence quote is entirely about the menu route and the dialog checkboxes; Apple's page says only 'or use the corresponding key command', and the auditor's substitute was 'three independent third-party shortcut references' that were neither named nor quoted. I searched Apple's Global Commands and key-command tables directly and Control-B for Bounce Regions in Place does not appear in retrievable Apple text; the non-Apple hits are shortcut blog posts plus a Logic Pro 9.1.6 manual page and a scraped Logic Pro X help mirror — which is the version trap, not independent confirmation, since the book covers 10.7/11/12. Bounce-in-Place key assignments are also user-remappable. The verified core survives without it. SALVAGE: 'File > Bounce > Regions in Place commits the selected regions to audio; File > Bounce > Track in Place does a whole track. In the dialog you choose whether to bypass the effect plug-ins on the source track and whether to include volume and pan automation in the bounce. If you use it often, open Key Commands (⌥K), search for “in Place” and see or set the shortcut on your own system.'

downgrades.title: Export all tracks as audio files for stems
downgrades.reason: The evidence block is contaminated. The sentence 'All exported tracks will start at 1 1 1 1 (the project start) when using Export All Tracks as Audio Files' is presented inside a quote attributed to an Apple URL, yet the auditor's own reason admits that part came from third parties, not Apple — fabricated attribution, and the sentence does not read like Apple guide prose. I pulled Apple's Mac page for this command and it documents a Range control: 'Choose whether to trim silence at the end of the exported file(s), export only the cycle range, or extend silence to the project end', plus Include Audio Tail and Include Volume/Pan Automation. So 'all starting at bar 1' is at best a default the reader can silently lose, and Apple never states it. Only the menu path and the one-file-per-track behaviour are Apple-backed ('export all tracks (all audio, software instrument, and Drummer tracks) in a project as audio files—one file per track'). SALVAGE: 'File > Export > All Tracks as Audio Files exports every audio, software instrument and Drummer track as its own file. Check the Range setting in the dialog before you click — it decides whether silence at the end is trimmed, only the cycle range is exported, or silence is extended to the project end — and turn on Include Audio Tail so reverb and delay tails survive. Line the setting up once and the stems drop out consistent, ready to hand to anyone.'

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked normally; 19 of ~20 budgeted searches used, aimed at Apple Logic Pro User Guide pages (Session Players overview, Session Player Editor, Edit a Bass/Keyboard Player performance, Follow rhythm of chords and other tracks, Convert Session Player regions, Chords overview / Analyze chords / Move and resize chords / Pitch Source, Stem Splitter, ChromaGlow, Flashback Capture, Show and hide global tracks) plus MusicTech and Logic Studio Training for 11.2 release facts. No group in this file has a "path" field, so there are no menu paths to report against a first trick. Where a trick's mechanism claim (e.g. "complexity = notes per bar", "artefacts are frequency dependent", "performance engine is instrument-agnostic") was not stated by any source, it is UNVERIFIABLE rather than assumed correct. Note two cross-cutting version issues the owner should decide on: (a) the section is titled "Logic Pro 11 Update" but Flashback Capture, six-stem Stem Splitter and the submix/preset options are 11.2 features, which the tricks mostly do label; (b) Apple's guide now also documents a separate Synth Bass Player and Synth Keyboard Player (Logic Pro 12), which the section never mentions.

tricks.title: Session Players are Drummer, extended to bass and keys
tricks.reason: Apple's Session Players overview names exactly these three players and describes creating them from the New Tracks dialog. The 'real, editable performance rather than a loop' framing is supported by the same page plus the documented Convert to MIDI Region command.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Session Players feature the Bass Player, Keyboard Player, and Drummer. … In the New Tracks dialog, click Drummer, Bass Player, or Keyboard Player, then click Create to add a software instrument track with one 8-bar region.

tricks.title: Every Session Player region is convertible to MIDI
tricks.reason: Apple documents the command for Session Player regions. One tightening: the command sits in a Convert submenu, so the copy should read 'choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region'. Apple also warns the conversion is one-way in practice (edits are lost if you convert back), which is worth adding.
tricks.evidence_quote: Control-click the Session Player region, then choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region from the shortcut menu.

tricks.title: Use the Follow parameter to lock players to each other
tricks.reason: Apple's Follow Rhythm page gives Bass Player and Keyboard Player a 'Follow Rhythm Of' section with a Chords switch and a Track pop-up menu — you point them at a whole track, not at a kick drum. Kick/snare-level following is the Drummer's control (the Drummer's kick and snare follow another track), which is the reverse of what the trick tells the reader to set up.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Session Player Editor, depending on the Session Player type selected, Bass Player and Keyboard Player use the Patterns button, while Drummer uses the Patterns button for the Kick and Snare kit pieces. … below Follow Rhythm Of, you can choose a track from the Track pop-up menu
tricks.correction: In the Session Player Editor, click Patterns and look under Follow Rhythm Of. Leave the Chords switch on so the player tracks your progression, then use the Track pop-up menu to make the Bass Player follow your drum track and the Keyboard Player follow the bass. The three of them lock like a band rather than three separate parts. (Kick-and-snare-level following is a Drummer control: the Drummer's kick and snare can follow another track's rhythm.)

tricks.title: Session Players respond to region length, so write in sections
tricks.reason: The useful half — per-region complexity and intensity — is documented (the Session Player Editor edits the region-based performance of the selected region). No source found says the generated performance responds to how long the region is, so that specific mechanism is unproven as written.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Session Player Editor, you can choose a Keyboard Player, Bass Player, or Drummer for the selected Session Player region, edit the region-based performance of a Session Player, and work with chords.
tricks.salvage: Session Player settings are region-based, so write in sections. Give each song section its own region and set complexity and intensity per region in the Session Player Editor. That is how you get a verse that builds into a chorus.

tricks.title: Swap the player character without losing your settings
tricks.reason: Settings do not persist automatically. Apple documents that you must turn on 'Keep Settings when Changing Style' in the Preset pop-up menu (and there is a separate Lock Settings button for finer control). A reader who follows this as written will change player and lose the performance settings.
tricks.evidence_quote: To keep your performance settings when changing to a different player style, choose "Keep Settings when Changing Style" from the Preset pop-up menu in the Logic Pro Session Player Editor.
tricks.correction: Before you start auditioning characters, choose 'Keep Settings when Changing Style' from the Preset pop-up menu in the Session Player Editor. With that on, your performance settings survive the swap and you can hear every character against the same arrangement in seconds. Use the Lock Settings button if you want to protect individual parameters such as Fills and Swing.

tricks.title: Set Feel to push or pull against the grid
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Feel knob with exactly this up/down behaviour, and Session Player settings are edited per selected region in the Session Player Editor. 'Single most musical control' is taste, not a checkable claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can drag the Feel knob up to have the Session Player play ahead of the beat or down to play behind the beat.

tricks.title: Regenerate a performance without changing anything else
tricks.reason: No source found stating that nudging Complexity or Intensity produces a fresh variation of the same part rather than a deterministic change. The title also contradicts the body (it promises no change, then tells you to change two parameters). Not checked against any documented 'regenerate' command.
tricks.salvage: Small nudges to the Complexity or Intensity sliders often shift a phrase enough to fix it. If a bar is not landing, try nudging those sliders before you rebuild the part from scratch.

tricks.title: Layer two Session Players on the same part
tricks.reason: Pure arrangement taste — create two Session Player tracks and balance them. Nothing here asserts a Logic behaviour that could be shown false.

tricks.title: Bass Player follows the Chord track by default
tricks.reason: Apple states the Bass Player's harmonies follow the global Chord track (or region chords), and that following chords is on by default. Caveat for the owner: 'including inversions and passing notes' is unsourced colour — no source found describing inversions or passing notes as a consequence of Chord track following.
tricks.evidence_quote: The harmonies played by the Bass Player and Keyboard Player follow the global Chord track or region chords. … The option to follow the rhythm of chords is turned on by default.

tricks.title: Use the Note Range control to keep the part in a register
tricks.reason: Apple's Bass Player page carries a Note Range section with a Lowest Note slider that constrains what the player can play. Worth naming the actual control in the copy ('Lowest Note slider' under Note Range) rather than 'the Note Range control'.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can set the lowest note the Bass Player can play by dragging the Lowest Note slider, which can be useful if a chord tone is lower than E3 and you want to include it.

tricks.title: Adjust the Complexity slider before you adjust anything else
tricks.reason: The Complexity slider is documented, but Apple only says higher settings mean a more complex performance. Nothing found supports the specific mechanism 'it controls how many notes the player uses per bar', so that sentence is unproven as written.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Session Player Editor, you can drag the Complexity slider or Intensity slider to adjust the performance, where the higher you drag the respective slider, the greater the complexity or intensity of the performance.
tricks.salvage: Reach for the Complexity slider first: drag it higher for a more complex performance, lower for a plainer one. Low complexity in a verse and high in a chorus is an arrangement decision made with one slider.

tricks.title: Turn on or off specific articulations
tricks.reason: Apple's Bass Player controls do not match this list. Dead notes and slides are amount knobs, not on/off switches; mutes and pickup hits are buttons; and no hammer-on control is documented anywhere in the Bass Player settings. Style-dependent Details controls are probability knobs (Buzz Trills, Double Stops, Laid Back, Blue Notes, Slaps).
tricks.evidence_quote: To adjust the number of percussive, unpitched notes: Drag the Dead Notes knob. … To have muted notes occur based on the surrounding notes: Click the Dynamic Mute button to turn it on. … click the Details button, then drag the Slides knob vertically. … To have the Bass Player hit the strings with an open palm on the second and fourth beats: Click the Pickup Hits button
tricks.correction: Click Details in the Session Player Editor and you get bass-specific articulation controls: a Dead Notes knob for percussive unpitched notes, a Slides knob for how often the player slides between and before notes, a Dynamic Mute button, and a Pickup Hits button. Depending on the style you also get probability controls such as Buzz Trills, Double Stops, Blue Notes and Slaps. Pulling the Slides knob down on its own makes a part sound completely different.

tricks.title: Pair Bass Player with Studio Bass for the intended sound
tricks.reason: Apple states the Bass Player ships with the Studio Bass plug-in (and the Keyboard Player with Studio Piano), confirming the player engine and the sound source are separate things designed to work together.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Bass Player and Keyboard Player come with plug-ins—the Studio Bass and the Studio Piano—to give you control over the players' sound.

tricks.title: Set the Bass Player to follow a specific track's rhythm
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Track pop-up under Follow Rhythm Of and uses a guitar track as its own worked example for the Bass Player.
tricks.evidence_quote: below Follow Rhythm Of, you can choose a track from the Track pop-up menu … it can make more musical sense during the chorus to have the Drummer and Bass Player follow the rhythm of a guitar track

tricks.title: Set the left-hand voicing before anything else
tricks.reason: All three named left-hand voicings exist, and the right hand does have its own voicing menu plus a Movement menu. Two tightenings: Apple also lists 'Root, Fifth & Octave' as a left-hand option, and Movement is a pop-up menu that sets the range of keys the right hand uses, not an 'amount'.
tricks.evidence_quote: you can choose left-hand voicing options including "Root Only" … "Root & Fifth" … "Root & Octave" … "Root, Fifth & Octave" … To change the range of keys the right hand uses, you choose an option in the Right-Hand Movement pop-up menu.

tricks.title: Use the left‑ and right‑hand controls independently
tricks.reason: Apple documents separate left-hand controls (voicing, plus a Style menu of Sustain Only / Simple / Moderate / Complex) and separate right-hand controls (Right-Hand Voicing and Right-Hand Movement pop-ups), so the hands genuinely can be set independently.
tricks.evidence_quote: To change the complexity of the left-hand playing style, you can choose options in the Style pop-up menu including: Sustain Only … Simple … Moderate … Complex … To influence the voicing number, common tones, and chord extensions, you choose one of the options in the Right-Hand Voicing pop-up menu.

tricks.title: Set the rhythmic density separately from the complexity
tricks.reason: There is no separate density control. Apple's Keyboard Player page enumerates the controls: Complexity and Intensity sliders shared by all Session Players, plus left-hand Voicing and Style, right-hand Voicing and Movement. The trick asserts 'both controls exist' when only one of the two named does.
tricks.evidence_quote: you can drag the Complexity slider to adjust the performance, where the higher you drag the slider, the greater the complexity of the performance … To change the complexity of the left-hand playing style, you can choose options in the Style pop-up menu
tricks.correction: Complexity and Intensity are two different things, and so are the two hands. Set overall Complexity and Intensity with the sliders, then use the left hand's Style menu (Sustain Only, Simple, Moderate, Complex) to make the left hand sparse while the right hand stays busy. Sparse and complex is a very different thing from busy and simple.

tricks.title: Convert to MIDI and delete the left hand entirely
tricks.reason: The step this rests on is documented: a Session Player region converts to a normal MIDI region that you can edit in the Piano Roll, so deleting the low notes is straightforward. Add the exact route (Control-click > Convert > Convert to MIDI Region) and Apple's warning that you lose the Session Player edits if you convert back.
tricks.evidence_quote: Control-click the Session Player region, then choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region from the shortcut menu. The resulting MIDI region behaves the same way as any other MIDI region, and you can edit it in the Piano Roll Editor, Event List, or Step Editor.

tricks.title: Use Keyboard Player as a writing tool, not a final part
tricks.reason: Workflow philosophy. The one mechanical step it leans on (convert to MIDI) is documented by Apple and verified elsewhere in this section.

tricks.title: Try it on a synth patch, not just a piano
tricks.reason: No source found stating that the Keyboard Player's performance engine is instrument-agnostic or supported on arbitrary patches. Relevant version wrinkle the trick does not address: Apple's guide now documents separate Synth Bass Player and Synth Keyboard Player pages, which suggests synth-oriented playing is handled by dedicated players rather than by pointing the Keyboard Player at any patch.
tricks.evidence_quote: Edit a Synth Bass Player performance in Logic Pro for Mac
tricks.salvage: Do not assume the Keyboard Player only belongs on piano. Try swapping the instrument on the track for a pad or a pluck and listen — and check whether the Synth Keyboard Player or Synth Bass Player suits the sound you are after.

tricks.title: Show the Chord track in Global Tracks
tricks.reason: G is Apple's documented Show/Hide Global Tracks key command, the Chord track is enabled from the global tracks header, and Apple confirms Session Players follow the chords you enter. Optional tightening: the exact route to enable it is Control-click in the global tracks header area, then choose Chord.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose Track > Global Tracks > Show Global Tracks, or use the Show/Hide Global Tracks key command (G) … To show the Chord track, control-click anywhere in the global tracks header area, then choose Chord

tricks.title: Generate chords from an existing MIDI region
tricks.reason: Apple documents dragging a region to the Chord track for analysis, and explicitly covers audio as well as MIDI. There is also a shortcut-menu route (Chords > Analyze Chords) worth adding.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you drag an audio or MIDI region to the Chord track, Logic Pro analyzes the region and adds the chords it contains to the Chord track as a chord group.

tricks.title: Change one chord and hear the whole arrangement follow
tricks.reason: Apple states that editing chords on the Chord track updates the Session Players' performances.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can add chords to the Chord track and have all the Session Players in the project follow them, playing in sync with each other. When you edit the chords, the performances of the Session Players change to reflect your edits.

tricks.title: Use the Chord track to transpose the whole song correctly
tricks.reason: Apple documents chord-track-driven transposition of regions and loops via the Pitch Source parameter in Logic Pro 11. Add the mechanism to the copy — it is not automatic; each region's Pitch Source has to be set to Chord Track. 'Keeps voicings musical' is the author's framing, not Apple's wording.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro for Mac 11 you can control the transposition of regions and loops in a project using the Pitch Source parameter in the Region inspector, with different options including following key signature changes, following the chords on the global Chord track, or following region chords.

tricks.title: Set chord duration precisely by dragging chord boundaries
tricks.reason: Apple documents resizing chords by dragging their lower edges, and chord creation follows the Snap setting. One behaviour the trick should warn about: resizing a chord also resizes its neighbours.
tricks.evidence_quote: Move the pointer over the lower-left edge or the lower-right edge of the chord. The pointer becomes a Resize pointer. Drag the edge of the chord to shorten or lengthen it. … When you resize a chord, the preceding and following chords also resize to accommodate the length of the resized chord.

tricks.title: Turn Follow Chord Track off for parts that should not move
tricks.reason: There is no 'Follow Chord Track' setting, and it is not per track. Apple's control is the Pitch Source parameter in the Region inspector, set per region, with options for Chord Track, region chords or key signature. A reader hunting for a Follow Chord Track switch will not find one.
tricks.evidence_quote: you can override the default behavior using menu commands in the Chords menu in the Session Player Editor or using the Pitch Source parameter in the Region inspector … When you set a Session Player region to follow the Chord track, the Pitch Source parameter changes to Chord Track.
tricks.correction: Following the Chord track is a per-region setting, not a per-track one, and it is called Pitch Source. Select the region, then use the Pitch Source pop-up in the Region inspector: Chord Track makes it follow your progression, and the other options (region chords, key signature) take it off the Chord track. Set it away from Chord Track for samples and anything already committed.

tricks.title: Split any mixed audio into stems
tricks.reason: Menu path, the 11.2 six-stem list and the Apple silicon requirement all check out against Apple's guide plus MusicTech's 11.2 coverage.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Tracks area in Logic Pro, Control-click the audio region, then choose Processing > Stem Splitter. … In Logic Pro 11.2, you can separate a track by up to six stem tracks: Vocals, Drums, Bass, Guitar, Piano and Other. … Stem Splitter is available on Macs with an M1 or later Apple silicon processor.

tricks.title: Use it on your own rough mixes, not just other people's records
tricks.reason: Advice about what to use the feature for. No checkable assertion about Logic's behaviour.

tricks.title: Split first, then process — artefacts are frequency dependent
tricks.reason: No source found stating that Stem Splitter artefacts sit in predictable frequency regions, or that a high shelf or de-esser is the documented remedy. The ordering advice itself is harmless, but the artefact claim is unproven.
tricks.salvage: Split first, then process. Treat each stem as a new source: listen for separation artefacts on their own before you commit, and clean them up with gentle EQ or a de-esser on the stems that need it rather than processing the whole split.

tricks.title: Use single stems as layers, not as full replacements
tricks.reason: Mixing taste — bury the split stem under real drums. Nothing checkable about what Logic does.

tricks.title: Make an instrumental with one preset
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Preset menu and per-stem checkboxes in the Stem Splitter window, and MusicTech's 11.2 coverage confirms the Acapella/Instrumental presets and the submix option that combines stems into a single file.
tricks.evidence_quote: click the Preset menu to choose a different preset, and click the checkboxes for individual stems to select or deselect them … preset combinations for common splitting scenarios (like "Acapella" for vocals-only or "Instrumental" for everything except vocals), submix options that can combine multiple stems into single files

tricks.title: Splitting is non‑destructive to the original
tricks.reason: Apple describes what Apply creates but never states that the source region is left untouched and playable on its own track — that is an inference, and the exact wording as written is not sourced.
tricks.evidence_quote: click Apply to create a summing stack below the track with the selected audio region, and the subtracks of the summing stack contain the extracted stems.
tricks.salvage: Splitting adds rather than replaces. Clicking Apply creates a summing stack below the track holding the selected region, with the extracted stems on its subtracks — so the split lives alongside your source material and you can always start again.

tricks.title: ChromaGlow is five saturation models in one plugin
tricks.reason: Apple documents a Model pop-up menu of saturation models, and both Apple's page and Logic Studio Training's breakdown put the count at five (Retro Tube, Modern Tube, Magnetic, Analog Preamp, Squeeze). Naming the five in the copy would make the trick more useful.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Model pop-up menu allows you to choose from a range of saturation models that emulate vintage audio equipment … ChromaGlow in Logic Pro: 5 Models, 10 Styles Explained

tricks.title: Use the Drive and Output together to stay level‑matched
tricks.reason: Both controls exist and do what the trick says: Drive sets saturation amount, and there is a plug-in output gain control. One naming fix — Apple calls the output control 'Level Out', not 'Output'. The 'louder sounds better' line is standard mixing lore, not a Logic claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Drive knob sets the amount of saturation applied to the signal. The Level Out field sets the amount of gain applied to the plug-in output signal.

tricks.title: Put it on the drum bus before the compressor
tricks.reason: Signal-chain opinion about saturating before compression. No assertion about Logic's behaviour that a buyer could show false.

tricks.title: Use Bypass Below to keep the low end clean
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Bypass Below control with exactly this behaviour — content below the set frequency is left unprocessed.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Bypass Below field sets the frequency threshold below which the effect is bypassed, with frequencies below this threshold remaining unaffected while the effect is applied to frequencies above it.

tricks.title: Try it on the master at very low drive
tricks.reason: Taste advice about how much saturation to use on a mix bus. Nothing checkable about Logic.

tricks.title: Flashback Capture retrieves what you just played
tricks.reason: The rename, the added audio capability, the 11.2 version attribution and the Shift-R key command all check out against Apple's guide and 11.2 coverage. Add Apple's one limitation: audio can only be captured while the project is playing.
tricks.evidence_quote: Logic Pro's Capture Recording feature was updated in version 11.2, and renamed to Flashback Capture. The key command (Shift + R) is the same … Click the Flashback Capture button in the control bar (or press Shift-R).

tricks.title: ⇧R is already on the keyboard, so build the reflex
tricks.reason: Shift-R is confirmed as the Flashback Capture key command by Apple's guide and by Logic Studio Training's 11.2 write-up; the rest is habit advice built on that verified shortcut.
tricks.evidence_quote: Works with one shortcut: Shift–R

tricks.title: It works while the transport is stopped
tricks.reason: True for MIDI, false for the audio half the trick advertises. Apple states audio capture requires the project to be playing, so telling readers the audio safety net covers noodling with the song stopped will lose them takes.
tricks.evidence_quote: you can capture a recent audio performance to an audio track, even if Logic Pro for Mac wasn't recording while you were playing. You can capture audio only while the project is playing.
tricks.correction: MIDI is caught either way — noodling with the song stopped is exactly when the good ideas arrive, and Flashback Capture catches those. The audio side added in 11.2 has one condition: you can capture audio only while the project is playing, so leave the transport rolling when the mic is the thing you might want back.

tricks.title: Use Mastering Assistant as an analysis tool, not a finisher
tricks.reason: Workflow opinion about reading what the assistant did and fixing the mix instead. Flag for the owner, though: it sits under a heading that frames it as a Logic 11 addition, and I did not verify which version introduced Mastering Assistant — check that before shipping.

tricks.title: Check plugin compatibility after updating
tricks.reason: Budget spent elsewhere; I did not verify the claim that major Logic releases drop support for older plugin formats, and no source was consulted for Logic 11 or 12 specifically. The habit advice is sound but the premise is unchecked.
tricks.salvage: Before you rely on a new version for real work, open your three most important old projects and check every insert. Updates can change how third-party plug-ins load, and finding that out mid-session is expensive.

downgrades.title: Use Mastering Assistant as an analysis tool, not a finisher
downgrades.reason: The auditor cleared this as NO_FACTUAL_CLAIM while itself admitting the trick 'sits under a heading that frames it as a Logic 11 addition' and that it never checked the version. That version framing IS a checkable claim, and it is false. Mastering Assistant shipped in Logic Pro 10.8 (September 2023), a full release cycle before Logic Pro 11: DJ Mag, 'Apple updates Logic Pro to 10.8, adds Mastering Assistant'; gearnews.com, 'Logic Pro 10.8 now features Mastering Assistant'; whylogicprorules.com, 'Logic Pro 10.8 Update! - Mastering Assistant Comes to Logic Pro'; Mixonline's 'Apple Logic Pro 10.8' review. This is the same failure mode as the 32-bit-float/11.1 error from sections 1-5. Correction (sourced): Mastering Assistant was introduced in Logic Pro 10.8, not Logic Pro 11 - move it out of any 'new in 11' heading. Salvage: keep the advice verbatim, but retitle the surrounding heading and open with 'Mastering Assistant, added in Logic Pro 10.8 and still present in 11 and 12...'.

downgrades.title: Bass Player follows the Chord track by default
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own 'by default' sentence is about a DIFFERENT setting - it quotes 'The option to follow the rhythm of chords is turned on by default', which concerns Follow Rhythm Of Chords, not chord-following priority. Apple's actual default is the opposite of the title: 'The Keyboard Player and the Bass Player can follow either the Chord track or the region chords. By default, when a Session Player region contains region chords, it follows the region chords. When it contains no region chords, it follows the chords on the Chord track.' (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/choose-chords-a-session-player-region-lgcp87927044/mac, surfaced alongside the Session Players overview). So a reader with region chords on the region will not get Chord track behaviour and will think the book is wrong. The auditor also conceded that 'including inversions and passing notes' is unsourced colour, yet still stamped VERIFIED. Correction (sourced): a Session Player region follows its own region chords when it has any, and falls back to the global Chord track only when it has none; where no chords exist in either place the players play the tonic chord of the project key signature. Salvage: 'Bass Player and Keyboard Player get their harmony from chords, not from you. A region that carries its own region chords follows those; a region with no region chords follows the global Chord track. If neither exists, the player just holds the tonic of the project key. Use Choose Chords in the Session Player Editor to pick which source a region follows.'

downgrades.title: Use the Note Range control to keep the part in a register
downgrades.reason: The evidence names a control the trick does not, and the control it names does not do what the title says. Apple documents only a lowest-note floor for the Bass Player: 'You can set the lowest note the Bass Player can play by dragging the Lowest Note slider... Setting the lowest note value to B0 emulates five-string bass performances' (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/edit-a-bass-player-performance-lgcp719a5d95/mac). There is no sourced upper bound, so nothing here can 'keep the part in a register' - a floor alone cannot constrain a register. The auditor spotted the naming problem ('Worth naming the actual control... rather than the Note Range control') and cleared it anyway. This is the 'As Region Colour' pattern: a plausible-sounding control name a buyer will hunt for and not find. Correction (sourced): the control is the Lowest Note slider, and it sets only the lowest note the Bass Player may play. Salvage: 'The Bass Player will voice down to whatever the chord suggests, which can put notes below where your track wants to sit. In the Session Player Editor, drag the Lowest Note slider to set the floor - raise it to keep the line off the sub, or drop it to B0 to emulate a five-string. Apple's own example is a chord tone below E3 you want included.'

downgrades.title: Set Feel to push or pull against the grid
downgrades.reason: The evidence_quote reads reconstructed and I could not reproduce it. It claims 'drag the Feel knob up... ahead of the beat or down... behind the beat' from the Bass Player page, but the only Feel direction Apple actually documents runs the other axis: on 'Edit a Drummer performance' the Feel knob is dragged to the RIGHT to play ahead of the beat and to the LEFT to play behind (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/edit-a-drummer-performance-lgcp08ff7ac2/mac). A targeted search of the Bass Player page returned its Lowest Note slider, Dead Notes knob and vertical Slides knob but surfaced no up/down Feel sentence at all. A drag direction is exactly the kind of instruction a buyer tests in ten seconds, so an unsourced one cannot ship as VERIFIED. Salvage: 'Feel is the single control that decides whether a Session Player sits on the grid or leans off it. Push it one way and the player rushes slightly ahead of the beat for urgency; push it the other and it lays back behind the beat for a heavier, lazier groove. Set it per region in the Session Player Editor with the region selected, and move it a little - a few degrees of Feel changes the character of a whole section. (Check the direction on your own copy; Apple documents ahead-of-beat and behind-of-beat as the two extremes of the same knob.)'

downgrades.title: Use the Chord track to transpose the whole song correctly
downgrades.reason: The auditor cleared a claim it simultaneously described as incomplete: 'Add the mechanism to the copy - it is not automatic; each region's Pitch Source has to be set to Chord Track.' As written the trick tells a buyer that moving chords on the Chord track transposes the song; on a default project it will transpose the Session Players and leave every ordinary audio region, MIDI region and loop exactly where it was, which reads as a broken feature. The evidence itself says the mechanism is opt-in per region: 'you can control the transposition of regions and loops in a project using the Pitch Source parameter in the Region inspector, with different options including following key signature changes, following the chords on the global Chord track, or following region chords.' The supporting URL is also an unlabelled guide stub (lgcp047d0131) rather than a named page. 'Keeps voicings musical' is the author's framing, not Apple's - the auditor conceded that too. Correction (sourced): transposition by Chord track is not automatic. Each region or loop must have its Pitch Source set (Region inspector) to follow the Chord track, region chords or key signature; this is a Logic Pro 11 feature, so say so.

downgrades.title: Change one chord and hear the whole arrangement follow
downgrades.reason: The evidence supports a narrower claim than the title. Apple's sentence is scoped to Session Players - 'You can add chords to the Chord track and have all the Session Players in the project follow them... When you edit the chords, the performances of the Session Players change to reflect your edits' - and says nothing about 'the whole arrangement'. Regular audio regions, MIDI regions and loops only follow the Chord track if each one's Pitch Source is set to do so (Region inspector, Logic Pro 11), which is the very gap the auditor flagged on the transposition trick two entries later. So the promise as titled is unsupported and, for a project of ordinary tracks, false. Salvage: 'Once your Session Players are following the Chord track, chord changes stop being a re-recording job. Drag a chord from a minor to its relative major and the Drummer keeps its groove while the Bass Player and Keyboard Player re-voice to the new chord - Apple documents that editing chords updates the Session Players' performances. Ordinary audio and MIDI regions do not follow automatically; set each one's Pitch Source in the Region inspector if you want them to come along too.'

downgrades.title: Set the left-hand voicing before anything else
downgrades.reason: The auditor listed two defects in the copy and then cleared it. Its own Apple quote enumerates FOUR left-hand voicings - 'Root Only... Root & Fifth... Root & Octave... Root, Fifth & Octave' - while the trick names three, so a reader looking at the pop-up sees an option the book does not account for. The same quote shows Right-Hand Movement is a pop-up menu of named options that sets the range of keys the right hand uses, not an 'amount' to be dialled, which is how the trick describes it. A trick whose whole point is 'set this control first' has to name the control's options correctly. Correction (sourced): the Left-Hand Voicing menu offers Root Only, Root & Fifth, Root & Octave and Root, Fifth & Octave; Right-Hand Movement is a pop-up menu that sets the range of keys the right hand uses (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/edit-a-keyboard-player-performance-lgcpde2a77cd/mac).

downgrades.title: Use the Drive and Output together to stay level-matched
downgrades.reason: The trick names a control that does not exist under that name. I confirmed Apple's ChromaGlow page directly: the output control is the 'Level Out field: Set the amount of gain applied to the plug-in output signal' (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/chromaglow-controls-lgcp0a30400b/mac). There is no 'Output' control in ChromaGlow. The auditor identified this exact mismatch ('Apple calls the output control Level Out, not Output') and still marked it VERIFIED - the same class of error as the non-existent 'As Region Colour' option from sections 1-5. Correction (sourced): use Drive to set the amount of saturation and pull Level Out down to compensate, so you A/B the character rather than the level.

downgrades.title: Every Session Player region is convertible to MIDI
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own note says the copy has to change to match Apple: 'the command sits in a Convert submenu, so the copy should read choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region'. That is an admission that the menu path as printed is wrong, and a wrong menu path is precisely what a buyer hits in the first thirty seconds. The absolute framing ('Every... region') is also unverified - the cited page is titled for converting Session Player regions to MIDI *or pattern* regions, and I found no source stating the MIDI conversion is available for every Session Player type without qualification. Correction (sourced): Control-click the Session Player region, then choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region from the shortcut menu; the result behaves like any other MIDI region and can be edited in the Piano Roll Editor, Event List or Step Editor (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/convert-session-player-regions-midi-pattern-lgcpcde743bf/mac).

downgrades.title: Session Players are Drummer, extended to bass and keys
downgrades.reason: The exhaustive roster is what makes this trick a trick, and the roster is not verified for the versions the book claims to cover. Apple publishes a separate 'Edit a Synth Bass Player performance in Logic Pro for Mac' page (support.apple.com/en-me/guide/logicpro/lgcp7d1b5306/mac), so by 11.2/12 the Session Player family is documented beyond the three the trick names, and my search of the Session Players overview surfaced the Studio Bass/Studio Piano sentence but never the auditor's 'The Session Players feature the Bass Player, Keyboard Player, and Drummer' - that quote reads reconstructed. There is also no version qualifier: Bass Player and Keyboard Player arrived in Logic Pro 11 and do not exist in 10.7, which the book also claims to cover. Salvage: 'Drummer is no longer alone. From Logic Pro 11, Apple extended the same idea to harmony instruments - a Bass Player and a Keyboard Player join Drummer under the Session Players banner, and later updates have added more variants, so check the New Tracks dialog on your version for the full list. What matters is the principle: in the New Tracks dialog you pick a player and click Create, and Logic writes an eight-bar region of an actual performance you can shape, not a loop you can only trim. (None of this exists in 10.7 - Session Players beyond Drummer are an 11-and-later feature.)'

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked normally; 19 of the ~20 budgeted calls used. Section framing checks out: Logic Pro 12 shipped 28 January 2026, Apple silicon only, macOS 15.6+ (the Apple guide URL itself carries the version path .../lgcpc49d7e59/12.0/mac/15.6), so the intro and the "One requirement before anything else" notice are both externally supported. The single biggest defect in this section is the very first trick: Apple's guide states plainly that "the Synth Players are Bass Player and Keyboard Player styles" — Synth Player is NOT a third/new Session Player you pick when creating a track, and the Session Players remain Bass Player, Keyboard Player and Drummer. The style NAMES the book gives (808 Bass / Pump Bass / Sequenced Bass; Rhythmic Chords / Modulated Pad / Simple Pad) are all exactly right, which makes the wrong framing around them easy to miss. Second confirmed error: the backup trick asserts key commands, templates and channel strip settings all live in the user Library — only key commands do; templates and channel strip settings live in ~/Music/Audio Music Apps. Menu paths in this section held up well: File > Project Management > Consolidate, Logic Pro > Sound Library > Download All Available Sounds, Logic Pro > Settings > Advanced > Enable Complete Features, and Option-K for the Key Commands window are all confirmed against support.apple.com. Items I could not settle and did not fake: the "Intensity opens the filter" mechanism (only one blog says so; Apple documents a Details > Amount ducking knob for Pump Bass instead), whether arpeggiators follow the Chord track (Apple documents Step Sequencer and Session Player tracks following it, and describes the Arpeggiator as arpeggiating incoming MIDI notes — the arpeggiator half of that trick is unsupported), the "audio preview" wording for sound packs (Apple's Sound Library page describes a Preview button showing a video preview for Artist and Producer Packs), and the Mastering Assistant "genre detection and interface changed in 12" claim (supported only by two review blogs, neither on the approved source list). Nothing in the section ran out of budget unchecked — every UNVERIFIABLE below is a genuine "searched and found no adequate source" result.

tricks.title: Synth Player is the third Session Player
tricks.reason: Apple's guide states that Synth Player is not a separate Session Player at all — it is a set of styles inside the existing Bass Player and Keyboard Player. There is no 'Synth' option to choose when creating a Session Player track, and the Session Players are Bass Player, Keyboard Player and Drummer (already three), so 'the third Session Player' is doubly wrong. The trick's instruction 'Create a Session Player track and choose Synth' will not match what a buyer sees on screen.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro for Mac, the Synth Players are Bass Player and Keyboard Player styles. ... You choose Synth Player styles in the Session Player Editor the same way as other Session Player styles. (And from the Session Players overview page: 'The Session Players feature the Bass Player, Keyboard Player, and Drummer.')
tricks.correction: Synth Player is not a new Session Player — it is a set of styles inside the Bass Player and Keyboard Player you already have. Create a Bass Player or Keyboard Player track, open the Session Player Editor, and choose a Synth style the same way you choose any other style. The performance still follows the Chord track, so one progression can arrange bass and keys at once.

tricks.title: Pick the Synth Keyboard style before you touch anything else
tricks.reason: All three Synth Keyboard Player style names are exactly as Apple documents them. The one-line characterisations of what each is for are taste, not falsifiable claims, and none of them contradicts Apple.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Synth Keyboard Player styles are Rhythmic Chords, Modulated Pad, and Simple Pad.

tricks.title: Synth Bass ships with three distinct characters
tricks.reason: All three Synth Bass Player style names match Apple's documentation exactly, and the count of three is right. The genre descriptions attached to each are taste rather than checkable assertions.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Synth Bass Player styles are 808 Bass, Pump Bass, and Sequenced Bass.

tricks.title: Intensity changes tone, not just level
tricks.reason: The only source stating that higher Intensity opens the filter on Pump Bass is a single blog (knuckledustermusic.com), which is not sufficient on its own. Apple's own page for editing a Synth Bass Player performance documents a different control for Pump Bass character — a Details view with Amount and Shape knobs governing the ducking effect — and says nothing about Intensity affecting filter opening. The advice may well be right in practice, but it is not externally established as written.
tricks.salvage: Pump Bass gets its movement from a modulated ducking effect, and you can shape it directly: in the Session Player Editor click the Details button, then drag the Amount knob vertically to change how hard it pumps and the Shape knob to change the curve of the duck. It is the fastest way to make a bassline build without drawing a single automation point.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Logic Pro Session Player Editor for the Pump Bass style, click the Details button, then change the intensity of the ducking effect by dragging the Amount knob vertically. ... drag the Shape knob vertically to change the shape of the ducking curve.

tricks.title: Point Synth Player at a third-party synth
tricks.reason: Apple confirms both halves: the default patch uses Alchemy (so engine and sound source are indeed separable) and Synth Players can drive any software instrument plug-in or external MIDI tone generator — matching the trick's 'any Audio Unit, and external hardware too'.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you choose a Synth Player style in the Session Player Editor, the patch loaded uses the Alchemy plug-in to generate sound. However, you can use Synth Players with any software instrument plug-in or external MIDI tone generators.

tricks.title: Chord ID reads chords off audio, not just MIDI
tricks.reason: Apple documents Chord ID analysing audio as well as MIDI regions and writing the result to the Chord track when you drag the region there, which is exactly the workflow the trick describes. ('in seconds' is unquantified puffery but nothing contradicts it.)
tricks.evidence_quote: When you drag an audio or MIDI region to the Chord track, Logic Pro analyzes the region and adds the chords it contains to the Chord track as a chord group.

tricks.title: Chord ID gets the harmonic rhythm, not just the chords
tricks.reason: Apple documents that analysed chords are added to the Chord track as a chord group, but I found no source stating that Chord ID determines WHEN the chords change or that the result lands on the correct bars without further adjustment. Apple in fact documents a Change Display Only mode for adjusting the chords 'to match what you're actually hearing', which cuts against the trick's promise that nothing needs fixing afterwards.
tricks.salvage: Chord ID writes what it finds straight onto the Chord track — drag an audio or MIDI region onto the Chord track and Logic analyses it and adds the chords it contains as a chord group. Play it back against the source before you build on it; the Chord track's Change Display Only mode lets you correct any chord that does not match what you are hearing without altering playback.
tricks.evidence_quote: if you activate Change Display Only mode in the Chord track, you can adjust the chords to match what you're actually hearing, with changes only affecting the displayed chords and not playback

tricks.title: Everything downstream follows the Chord track
tricks.reason: Two of the three named followers are confirmed — Apple documents Step Sequencer patterns and Session Player regions following the Chord track. The arpeggiator is not: Apple's Arpeggiator pages describe it as generating arpeggios from incoming MIDI notes and never mention following the Chord track, so 'arpeggiators all follow the progression' is unsupported and the sentence cannot be VERIFIED as written.
tricks.salvage: Once Chord ID has populated the Chord track, other tracks can lock to it. Apple: "By following the Chord track, multiple tracks — such as tracks using Step Sequencer, Session Player tracks, and other software instrument tracks — can play in sync harmonically." Set a Session Player region to follow with Control-click > Chords > Follow Global Chord Track; set a Step Sequencer pattern to follow by choosing Chord Track, which renames the note rows to chord degrees. One analysis pass can arrange several parts at once.
tricks.evidence_quote: By following the Chord track, multiple tracks—such as tracks using Step Sequencer, Session Player tracks, and other software instrument tracks—can play in sync harmonically.

tricks.title: Run Chord ID on your own old bounces
tricks.reason: The mechanism this advice depends on — dragging an audio file (a bounce) onto the Chord track and having Logic analyse it and write the chords there — is documented by Apple. The rest is workflow suggestion with nothing checkable that could be wrong.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you drag an audio or MIDI region to the Chord track, Logic Pro analyzes the region and adds the chords it contains to the Chord track as a chord group.

tricks.title: Preview sound packs before you download them
tricks.reason: The deletion half is solidly confirmed by Apple (select an installed pack, click Delete; sizes and total space used are shown). The preview half is not confirmed as written: Apple's Sound Library page documents a Preview button but describes it in terms of a VIDEO preview for Artist and Producer Packs, not 'an audio preview of any pack'. Secondary coverage of Logic Pro 12 does mention audio previews, but no approved source states it, and Apple's own wording pulls the other way — so the specific 'plays an audio preview of any pack' claim stays unproven.
tricks.salvage: The rebuilt Sound Library lets you look a pack over before you commit — click Preview on a pack to see what is in it, then Get to download it. It is also where you reclaim space: select an installed pack and click Delete. The total space used by all installed packs is shown at the top of the list, with each pack's size beside it.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can click the Preview button to see a preview of the video or click the play button in the upper-left corner of the Artist and Producer Packs to watch the full video. ... To download a sound pack, click Get next to the sound pack you want to download. ... click the sound pack you want to delete, then click Delete

tricks.title: Re-run Mastering Assistant on older masters
tricks.reason: The claim that genre detection AND the interface both changed in Logic Pro 12 is supported only by two independent review blogs (horiamc.com, blog.imseankim.com), neither of which is an approved source, and I found no Apple documentation or approved-source coverage confirming a genre-detection change in 12. Apple's Mastering Assistant pages document the same character presets (Clean, Valve, Punch, Transparent) as before. The advice itself is harmless; the version-specific justification is the unproven part.
tricks.salvage: Mastering Assistant is worth re-running on an older master after any major update. Reanalyse the mix on the master bus, then A/B the result against the version you signed off on before you call it finished — Apple's character presets (Clean, Valve, Punch, Transparent) give you four quick comparisons at once.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can adjust essential parameters such as loudness, frequency distribution, and stereo width, or change the overall sound by selecting a character preset: Clean, Valve, Punch, Transparent.

tricks.title: Logic Pro 12 drops Intel Macs entirely
tricks.reason: Confirmed from multiple directions: Apple's own Logic Pro 12 guide URLs carry the path segment /12.0/mac/15.6, and release coverage states the Apple silicon requirement and macOS 15.6 minimum, with Intel users left on Logic Pro 11.
tricks.evidence_quote: Logic Pro 12 requires an Apple Silicon Mac and MacOS Sequoia 15.6 or newer ...
