This is the first version of Logic Pro that no longer supports Intel Macs (logicpros.net; corroborated by production-expert.com, 'Logic Pro 12: AI Features, New Tools And Intel Mac Support Dropped')

tricks.title: Never update in the middle of a paid project
tricks.reason: Pure workflow judgement about when to update. No assertion about what Logic Pro does that a buyer could test and dispute.

tricks.title: Keep the previous version installed alongside the new one
tricks.reason: No source supports the specific method given — duplicating Logic Pro in Applications, renaming the copy, and 'macOS will run both'. Apple documents a materially different procedure for keeping an outgoing version: compress the app to a zip and store it in a version-named folder inside Applications, then unzip and drag it back to Applications when you want to use it, which is a swap rather than two live installs. Since a buyer following the book's steps may not get the behaviour promised, the advice should be re-pointed at Apple's documented route.
tricks.salvage: Keep the outgoing version before you update, using Apple's own procedure: make a folder inside Applications named for the version (for example "Logic Pro 11.1.2"), select Logic Pro and choose File > Compress "Logic Pro", then move the resulting Logic Pro.zip into that folder. If the new version gives you trouble, unzip that copy and drag it into Applications and you are back where you were.
tricks.evidence_quote: Create a new folder in the Applications folder and name the folder with the name and version of the application (for example, "Logic Pro 11.1.2"). Select the Logic Pro application in the Applications folder and choose File > Compress "Logic Pro". Move the resulting "Logic Pro.zip" file into the folder you created.

tricks.title: Back up your key commands, templates and channel strip settings
tricks.reason: The claim that all three 'live in your user Library' is false for two of the three. Key commands do live there (~/Library/Application Support/Logic/Key Commands, which is where the export dialog points). Project templates and channel strip settings live in ~/Music/Audio Music Apps — a buyer following this trick would go looking in the wrong folder and conclude their templates were gone. The export instruction itself is correct.
tricks.evidence_quote: Channel Strip Settings are stored on the internal startup drive in the folder Music→Audio Music Apps→Channel Strip Settings. (And macprovideo.com, 'The Joys, And Benefits, Of Building Templates In Logic Pro X': custom templates are saved into a Project Templates folder in ~/Music/Audio Music Apps. Apple's Key Commands page: 'choose Options > Export Key Commands in the Key Commands window. A dialog opens, pointing to the default folder location: ~/Library/Application Support/Logic/Key Commands.')
tricks.correction: Key commands are the only one of these that lives in your user Library. Open the Key Commands window (Option-K), choose Options > Export Key Commands, and save the file somewhere safe — the dialog defaults to ~/Library/Application Support/Logic/Key Commands. Your templates and channel strip settings live somewhere else entirely: ~/Music/Audio Music Apps/Project Templates and ~/Music/Audio Music Apps/Channel Strip Settings. Copy those two folders as well.

tricks.title: Consolidate and archive your three most important projects
tricks.reason: The menu path is exactly as Apple documents it, and Apple explicitly frames Consolidate as the way to make a project safe to move or archive — which is precisely the use the trick puts it to.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose File > Project Management > Consolidate (or use the Consolidate Project key command) ... This ensures that if you move or copy the project to another computer, or archive the project for later use, the assets remain with the project and are accessible.

tricks.title: Check your critical third‑party plugins against the new version first
tricks.reason: General advice about third-party developers' release timing and checking compatibility pages. It makes no checkable assertion about Logic Pro's behaviour.

tricks.title: Note your current I/O and buffer settings
tricks.reason: The advice rests on the assertion that 'major updates sometimes reset audio device preferences', and I found no source establishing that Logic Pro updates reset audio device settings. The screenshot habit is sound regardless, so the trick survives with the causal claim removed.
tricks.salvage: Screenshot your Audio settings before you update — output device, input device and I/O buffer size. It takes five seconds, and if anything about your setup looks different afterwards you can restore the exact configuration you were working with instead of guessing at it.

tricks.title: Update macOS and Logic separately, a week apart
tricks.reason: Pure troubleshooting discipline — change one variable at a time. Nothing checkable about Logic Pro.

tricks.title: Open an old project and audit every insert
tricks.reason: Workflow advice: check your plug-ins after an update before trusting the migration. It asserts nothing specific about Logic Pro's behaviour that a buyer could disprove.

tricks.title: Rebuild your templates rather than opening old ones
tricks.reason: Taste and workflow. The general observation that new versions add track types and defaults an old template will not carry is not a specific checkable claim about any named feature.

tricks.title: Re-check Enable Complete Features after updating
tricks.reason: Apple documents exactly this control at exactly this path in the current guide, and describes exactly the symptom the trick warns about — with it off, Logic runs in Simplified mode and whole areas of the program (Event/Marker/Tempo/Signature lists, Project Audio and All Files browsers, Step Editor, expanded mixing and automation) are unavailable. Note the path is 'Settings', not the old 'Preferences', which is correct for the versions this book covers.
tricks.evidence_quote: Go to Logic Pro > Settings > Advanced, then select the Enable Complete Features checkbox. When selected, advanced features such as project alternatives and backups, beat mapping, expanded mixing and automation capabilities, and more are available.

tricks.title: Read the new Key Commands list for additions
tricks.reason: The key command itself is confirmed — Option-K opens the Key Commands window. But 'sort by command name' is not supported by any source I found; Apple documents opening, browsing, importing and exporting key commands but not a sortable command-name column, so the instruction as written may send a buyer looking for a control that is not there. The trick works fine once that step is dropped.
tricks.salvage: Open the Key Commands window after every update — Logic Pro > Key Commands > Edit, or Option-K — and read through it for commands you have not seen before. New features arrive with new commands, many of them unassigned by default, and this is the only place they announce themselves.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can open the Key Commands window by choosing Logic Pro > Key Commands > Edit or by pressing Option-K.

tricks.title: Run the Sound Library update fully before working
tricks.reason: The menu path is exactly as Apple documents it. The 'silent tracks that look fine' aside is a consequence framing rather than a separate checkable claim, and nothing contradicts it.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, you can choose Logic Pro > Sound Library > Download All Available Sounds.

tricks.title: Test your bounce path end to end before you need it
tricks.reason: Advice to rehearse your delivery formats before a deadline. No assertion about Logic Pro that could be shown false.

tricks.title: Give yourself a deliberate hour to explore
tricks.reason: Pure learning advice with nothing checkable in it.

downgrades.title: Re-check Enable Complete Features after updating
downgrades.reason: The evidence supports an adjacent claim, not the claim as written. The trick's operative assertion is that an update can switch Enable Complete Features OFF, so you should re-check it afterwards. Apple's page documents only what the checkbox does and what Simplified mode lacks; nothing in it says updating Logic resets the setting. That causal premise is the entire reason the trick exists and it has zero external support. Two further problems the auditor missed: (a) the auditor asserted 'the path is Settings, not the old Preferences, which is correct for the versions this book covers' -- that is false for Logic Pro 10.7, one of the three versions the book claims to cover, where Apple's own page is titled 'Advanced preferences in Logic Pro' and the route is Logic Pro > Preferences > Advanced (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/advanced-preferences-lgcpb6dcc6fa/10.7/mac/11.0). This matters because the group heading is the generic 'After you update' and the section intro explicitly widens scope to 'surviving any major release', so a 10.7 reader is in scope. (b) The body's claim that the pane 'holds a single Enable Complete Features checkbox' -- i.e. that it contains only that one control -- is unverified. SALVAGE (keeps the genuinely verified part, drops the unproven cause): 'If half the program seems to have disappeared -- no Event or Marker lists, no Step Editor, no project alternatives -- check Logic Pro > Settings > Advanced and make sure Enable Complete Features is ticked. With it off, Logic runs in Simplified mode and a Simplified badge appears at the right of the control bar. On Logic Pro 10.7 the same control lives under Logic Pro > Preferences > Advanced.'

downgrades.title: Run the Sound Library update fully before working
downgrades.reason: I confirmed the menu path verbatim ('In Logic Pro, choose Logic Pro > Sound Library > Download All Available Sounds', https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/download-additional-sound-packs-lgcp8b3abc1c/mac), so that half is sound. But the auditor waved away the second sentence -- 'A half-downloaded library produces silent tracks that look fine' -- as 'consequence framing rather than a separate checkable claim'. That is exactly backwards: it is the only falsifiable mechanism claim in the trick, and it is the reason a reader would act on it. It asserts a specific silent-failure mode (audio absent, UI showing no problem) that no Apple page documents. Apple's own troubleshooting material on missing content describes prompts and unavailable-content notices, not tracks that play silently while looking normal. Unsourced and plausibly false. SALVAGE (verified route, unproven symptom removed): 'Before you start work on a fresh install, choose Logic Pro > Sound Library > Download All Available Sounds and let it finish. Patches that depend on content you have not downloaded yet will not load properly, and chasing that mid-session wastes an afternoon.'

downgrades.title: Rebuild your templates rather than opening old ones
downgrades.reason: Downgraded from NO_FACTUAL_CLAIM: this smuggles in a checkable mechanism claim about what Logic does. The body states 'New versions add track types, settings and defaults that an old template will not have' and that rebuilding means 'you get every new default for free'. That is an assertion about how Logic handles template/project files across versions, not taste -- and it is doubtful on its face, since a template is just a project file and opening it in a newer Logic does not strip newly added features, while most new global defaults come from Settings rather than from the template. No source establishes that an old template withholds new defaults or that rebuilding confers them. SALVAGE (advice retained, mechanism claim dropped): 'After a major update, build a fresh template from a new empty project rather than carrying the old one forward. It takes about an hour, it forces you to notice what has changed, and it is a good moment to prune the tracks and busses you stopped using two projects ago.'

downgrades.title: Open an old project and audit every insert
downgrades.reason: Downgraded from NO_FACTUAL_CLAIM. The auditor said it 'asserts nothing specific about Logic Pro's behaviour that a buyer could disprove', but the instruction is 'Look for greyed-out or missing plugins on every channel' -- a specific claim about how Logic renders unavailable or failed-to-load plug-ins after a migration. Whether Logic greys such slots out (versus italicising them, showing a placeholder, throwing a dialog on load, or silently dropping them) is checkable and unsourced. A buyer who updates, sees no greyed-out slots, and assumes everything migrated has been misled by the trick's own detection criterion. SALVAGE (advice retained, unverified visual cue dropped): 'Before you trust the migration, open a finished older project and step through every channel strip, checking each insert actually loads and reports its plug-in name. Play the project back against a bounce you made under the previous version -- if something failed to instantiate, the difference is audible even when the session looks intact.'
